system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 8 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2184-10-27 18:43:00 to 2184-11-04 10:46:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of mitochondrial myopathy, coronary artery disease with multiple prior stents, hypertension, and dyslipidemia was admitted for evaluation of sudden-onset chest pain at rest, which resolved with sublingual nitroglycerin. He also reported labile blood pressure and orthostatic hypotension. Initial ECG and serial troponins were normal, ruling out acute myocardial infarction. A chest X-ray showed no acute abnormalities. He underwent an exercise stress MIBI test, which revealed ischemic ECG changes during exertion but normal myocardial perfusion and a preserved ejection fraction of 52%. The known 70% stenosis in the PDA was deemed unsuitable for intervention. He was treated with IV fluids for mild dehydration related to his mitochondrial myopathy, with improvement in creatinine from 1.4 to 1.2 mg/dL. Blood pressure management was optimized by switching from oral clonidine to a weekly patch and increasing isosorbide mononitrate to 30 mg daily. He remained in normal sinus rhythm, with no arrhythmic events. He was discharged home with medication adjustments and instructions to follow up with cardiology.
problems: Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery
Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, unspecified, with chronic kidney disease stage I through stage IV, or unspecified

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ is a ___ year old gentleman with history of 
mitochondrial myopathy, coronary artery disease, hypertension, 
and dyslipidemia presenting from clinic with hypotension, with 
development of chest pain in ED.  

# Orthostatic Hypotension 
He was noted to have hypotension and bradycardia in setting of 
receiving his home blood pressure medications. His medications 
were held with some improvement in his symptoms.  When restarted 
on valsartan and isosorbide mononitrate, patient exhibited a 60 
point drop in systolic blood pressure from supine to standing, 
with BP ___ while standing, so medications were held again 
and patient was given IV fluids. He was felt to be dehyradated 
due to Uosm >600, Sosm <300. He was aggressively hydrated by 
intravenous fluids as oral hydration did not appear to succeed. 
With hydration the patient remained orthostatic, but with 
improved upright blood pressure which allowed him to walk and 
function without symptoms. His valsartan was restarted, titrated 
to standing systolic blood pressure 140s, though he had been 
hypertensive to 180s while supine.  He was discharged on half 
the dose of metoprolol succinate as he was taking previously in 
addition to home dose of valsartan.  He will follow up with his 
cardiologist Dr. ___ week, at which time his isosorbide 
mononitrate can be restarted.  His diltiazem was also held 
during this hospitalization and on discharge in the setting of 
bradycardia.  He should not be restarted on his clonidine. 

Patient noted that he has frequent episodes of dehydration for 
which he needs to be admitted to the hospital every six weeks.  
It was recommended that he follow-up with Dr. ___ to 
investigate any evidence for malabsortion which can explain his 
apparent inability to hydrate orally.  It was also recommended 
for him to follow up with Dr. ___ in ___ clinic 
for further workup as an outpatient for possible autonomic 
dysfunction in the setting of his mitochondrial disease. 

# Chest Pain 
Mr. ___ was admitted for chest pain in the ED and had a few 
more episodes during hospitalization. He does have a significant 
history of coronary artery disease s/p PCI x multiple with last 
PCI last fall in ___.  Last stress test was in ___ 
showing ECG changes but no perfusion defects.  He was monitored 
on telemetry and ruled out for myocardial infarction with 
multiple sets of negative cardiac enzymes.  ECGs were reviewed, 
showing minimal change since prior from ___. There did 
appear to be < 1mm STE in V2, slightly less in V1 and V3 in the 
absence of chest pain. Episodes of chest pain appeared to be 
associated with demand in setting of orthostasis, often occuring 
while patient was dehydrated and orthostatic.  Episodes were 
self-resolving. 

# Hypertension
Patient has history of hypertension, which he states has been 
labile for several months, difficult to control, requiring 
multidrug regimen including clonidine.  Medications were held 
during hospitalization in setting of significant orthosasis and 
slowly restarted.  Upon discharge, patient's blood pressures 
were elevated, though still orthostatic with systolics up to 
180s while supine and 150s while standing.  He is reasonably 
very concerned about the effect of hypertension on his kidneys, 
though we could not restart any further medications at this time 
in setting of symptomatic orthosasis.  Isosorbide mononitrate 
will likely be restarted next week in clinic. 

# Acute on Chronic Renal Insufficiency
Patient's baseline creatinine appeared to be 1.2, and he 
presented with creatinine elevated to 1.5.  With aggressive IV 
fluids, his creatinine improved to 1.1 by discharge.  As 
mentioned above, patient notes frequent readmissions for 
dehydration requiring IV hydration for days.

bradycardia.  He should not be restarted on his clonidine. 

Patient noted that he has frequent episodes of dehydration for 
which he needs to be admitted to the hospital every six weeks.  
It was recommended that he follow-up with Dr. ___ to 
investigate any evidence for malabsortion which can explain his 
apparent inability to hydrate orally.  It was also recommended 
for him to follow up with Dr. ___ in ___ clinic 
for further workup as an outpatient for possible autonomic 
dysfunction in the setting of his mitochondrial disease. 

# Chest Pain 
Mr. ___ was admitted for chest pain in the ED and had a few 
more episodes during hospitalization. He does have a significant 
history of coronary artery disease s/p PCI x multiple with last 
PCI last fall in ___.  Last stress test was in ___ 
showing ECG changes but no perfusion defects.  He was monitored 
on telemetry and ruled out for myocardial infarction with 
multiple sets of negative cardiac enzymes.  ECGs were reviewed, 
showing minimal change since prior from ___. There did 
appear to be < 1mm STE in V2, slightly less in V1 and V3 in the 
absence of chest pain. Episodes of chest pain appeared to be 
associated with demand in setting of orthostasis, often occuring 
while patient was dehydrated and orthostatic.  Episodes were 
self-resolving. 

# Hypertension
Patient has history of hypertension, which he states has been 
labile for several months, difficult to control, requiring 
multidrug regimen including clonidine.  Medications were held 
during hospitalization in setting of significant orthosasis and 
slowly restarted.  Upon discharge, patient's blood pressures 
were elevated, though still orthostatic with systolics up to 
180s while supine and 150s while standing.  He is reasonably 
very concerned about the effect of hypertension on his kidneys, 
though we could not restart any further medications at this time 
in setting of symptomatic orthosasis.  Isosorbide mononitrate 
will likely be restarted next week in clinic. 

# Acute on Chronic Renal Insufficiency
Patient's baseline creatinine appeared to be 1.2, and he 
presented with creatinine elevated to 1.5.  With aggressive IV 
fluids, his creatinine improved to 1.1 by discharge.  As 
mentioned above, patient notes frequent readmissions for 
dehydration requiring IV hydration for days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I’m Dr. ___. I understand you came in because of low blood pressure and feeling weak. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been feeling off for a few days—just weak and kind of faint. My blood pressure was 85 over 60 at my cardiologist’s office. It’s been all over the place lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned some chest pressure in the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it came on while I was coming here. Felt like pressure, lasted about an hour, then went away on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve checked your EKG and cardiac enzymes, and there’s no sign of a heart attack. Your labs also show your kidney function is a bit worse than usual—creatinine is 1.5, up from your baseline of 1.2.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That happens when I get dehydrated. I end up in the hospital every six weeks or so for IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your urine is very concentrated, which tells us you’re dehydrated. We’re going to give you IV fluids to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s usually what helps. But why is my blood pressure so low now? It was 170 over 90 just last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is very labile—meaning it swings a lot. And some of your medications, like clonidine and isosorbide, can lower it too much, especially when you're dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So should I stop them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, we’re holding your clonidine, diltiazem, and isosorbide. We’ll restart them slowly once your hydration improves and we can monitor your response.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the chest pain—was that from my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t think it was a heart attack. Your enzymes were negative, and your EKG didn’t show major changes. But you do have known coronary disease, so we’re watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had stents before. Last stress test showed changes but no blockage in blood flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. So the chest pressure may have been from your heart working harder during dehydration and low blood pressure—what we call ‘demand ischemia.’

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I felt worse when I stood up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we confirmed orthostatic hypotension—your BP drops significantly when you stand. That’s why you feel faint.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from my mitochondrial disease?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. It can affect your autonomic nervous system, which controls blood pressure. We’re recommending you follow up with a specialist to look into that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’d like that. I also started iron—my ferritin was low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your ferritin was 26, which is low, but your iron ratio is normal. We’ll keep you on ferrous gluconate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood work from overnight looks stable. No infection—blood and urine cultures are negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a little stronger already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is starting to come down—now 1.3—so the fluids are helping your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But I’m worried—why can’t I stay hydrated just by drinking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. It could be related to your mitochondrial disease causing osmotic diuresis. We’re recommending a GI workup to check for malabsorption.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll follow up on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We restarted your valsartan this morning. We’ll watch your BP closely. If it stays stable, we may restart metoprolol at a lower dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You’re lowering my metoprolol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to 25 mg once daily instead of 50 mg twice. Your heart rate has been low, and with your history of bradycardia, we want to be cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about the clonidine and diltiazem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not restarting clonidine. It’s likely contributing to your low BP. Diltiazem is also being held due to bradycardia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ve had side effects from clonidine before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is now 1.1—back to your baseline. That’s great. Your BP is still labile, but standing pressures are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not feeling as dizzy when I stand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re going to keep you on the lower metoprolol dose and continue valsartan. Isosorbide will be restarted at your cardiology follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I should keep taking the iron?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, twice daily. We’ll monitor your levels at your next visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. No more chest pain, and your telemetry shows no arrhythmias.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow if your BP stays stable. You’ll follow up with your cardiologist next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ll make sure to keep that appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you today. Your kidney function has improved, and you’re walking without dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What changes are we making to my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stop clonidine and diltiazem. Isosorbide is paused for now. Metoprolol is now 25 mg once daily. Valsartan continues twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the aspirin and statin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue as before—atorvastatin at bedtime, clopidogrel daily, and now chewable aspirin twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And I should watch my blood pressure at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially when standing. Call your doctor if you feel dizzy or if your systolic drops below 100.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I’ll follow up for the autonomic testing and GI evaluation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Those are important to prevent future hospitalizations.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in—how are you feeling at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pretty good. BP is higher when lying down—around 170—but 140 when standing. Not dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. The difference will likely improve over time. Keep up with fluids and your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I’ve scheduled the autonomic clinic visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge. Your condition has stabilized, and you’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the help. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: no clonidine, lower metoprolol, and follow up next week to possibly restart isosorbide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve got it written down. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re officially discharging you. Your kidney function is normal, and your blood pressure is manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go. I’ll follow all the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Stay hydrated, monitor your BP, and keep your appointments. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers and prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—call us if you have chest pain, severe dizziness, or your BP drops too low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I know the signs now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’ve done really well this admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I feel like I understand my condition better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s our goal. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at the follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll be expecting you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy the first few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. No overexertion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. Listen to your body.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve learned that the hard way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad you’re feeling better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Me too. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with mitochondrial myopathy, coronary artery disease, and a history of orthostatic hypotension was admitted for evaluation of hypotension and chest pain. He presented from cardiology clinic with systolic blood pressure as low as 85, presyncope, and self-resolving chest pressure. Initial workup ruled out acute myocardial infarction, with normal cardiac enzymes and EKGs showing only minimal changes. He was found to have acute kidney injury with creatinine rising from baseline 1.2 to 1.5, attributed to chronic dehydration from his mitochondrial disorder. He received IV fluids, which improved renal function to creatinine 1.1. His blood pressure medications—clonidine, diltiazem, and isosorbide mononitrate—were held due to symptomatic orthostasis and bradycardia. Metoprolol was reduced to 25 mg daily. Valsartan was continued. He was discharged home with plans to follow up for autonomic dysfunction and GI evaluation for malabsorption, with instructions to restart isosorbide mononitrate in clinic.
